prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: defendant officer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an officer's use of a taser on an actively resisting suspect does not violate clearly established Fourth Amendment law.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Officer is entitled to qualified immunity because he did not violate clearly established Fourth Amendment law.**

Qualified immunity shields an officer unless (1) he violated a constitutional right and (2) that right was "clearly established" when he acted. *Pearson v. Callahan*, 555 U.S. 223, 232 (2009). A court may begin with the second question. *Id.* at 236. Plaintiff bears the burden of showing that the right was clearly established. A right is clearly established only if its contours are "sufficiently clear that every reasonable official would have understood that what he is doing violates that right." *Ashcroft v. al-Kidd*, 563 U.S. 731, 741 (2011) (cleaned up). Courts must not define clearly established law "at a high level of generality." *Id.* at 742. Plaintiff must therefore identify controlling authority that put the unlawfulness of this particular use of force "beyond debate." *Id.* at 741.

**A. Excessive-force claims turn on the suspect's resistance.**

Excessive-force claims are judged by objective reasonableness. The inquiry weighs the severity of the crime, the threat the suspect posed, and whether he was actively resisting or evading arrest. *Graham v. Connor*, 490 U.S. 386, 396 (1989). The Sixth Circuit applies these factors to Taser use. It has repeatedly held that an officer may use a Taser to subdue a suspect who is actively resisting. It has denied immunity only where the suspect was subdued, compliant, or not resisting. *See Hagans v. Franklin Cnty. Sheriff's Off.*, 695 F.3d 505, 509 (6th Cir. 2012); *Rudlaff v. Gillispie*, 791 F.3d 638, 641–42 (6th Cir. 2015).

That distinction is dispositive here. The record shows that Plaintiff was not passive. He [describe specific conduct: refused commands, pulled away, struggled, etc.] before Officer deployed the Taser. Active resistance of that kind is the circumstance in which this Circuit has found Taser use reasonable.

**B. Sixth Circuit precedent confirms that Taser use against an actively resisting suspect is not clearly unlawful.**

In *Hagans*, the court granted immunity where the officer used a Taser on a suspect who refused to comply with the officer's efforts to control him. The court found no clearly established law that such force was excessive. 695 F.3d at 509–11. In *Rudlaff*, the court again held that officers who used a Taser while a suspect was resisting did not violate clearly established law. 791 F.3d at 641–44. In *Kent v. Oakland County*, 810 F.3d 384, 391–92 (6th Cir. 2016), the court reached the same conclusion. It treated the suspect's continued resistance as the key fact. It held that force used to overcome that resistance did not violate a clearly established right. *Goodwin ex rel. Nall v. City of Painesville*, 781 F.3d 314, 321–22 (6th Cir. 2015), likewise recognized that officers may use a Taser to gain control of a noncompliant suspect who is actively resisting. *See also Bletz v. Gribble*, 641 F.3d 743, 755 (6th Cir. 2011) (analyzing Taser use under the *Graham* factors and the suspect's resistance).

*Mullins v. Cyranek*, 805 F.3d 760, 766 (6th Cir. 2015), confirms where the line falls. Force used while a suspect resists is evaluated differently from force used after he is subdued. Here, Officer used the Taser during the struggle and stopped once Plaintiff was under control. [Confirm against the record.] Officer's conduct falls on the permissible side of the line that these cases draw.

**C. Plaintiff cannot identify controlling authority that clearly establishes a violation on these facts.**

Plaintiff must point to a case that places the constitutional question beyond debate. The cases that deny immunity involve suspects who were handcuffed, compliant, or otherwise not resisting. They do not clearly establish that Taser use against a suspect who is actively resisting is unlawful. A reasonable officer reading *Hagans*, *Rudlaff*, *Kent*, and *Goodwin* would have understood that using a Taser to overcome active resistance is permissible. At a minimum, those decisions show that the law did not give Officer fair warning that his conduct was unconstitutional. Because no clearly established law prohibited Officer's conduct, he is entitled to qualified immunity.

**Conclusion.** The Court should hold that Officer is entitled to qualified immunity and reverse the denial of his motion. [Adjust the relief to the procedural posture.]
